utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Cont'd]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Gelic, a number of documents to look at quickly to identify the sort of documents you were preparing. May we distribute 2818, which is a clip of documents covering several months. While they are being distributed: Major, do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as much as is sufficient for me. I can understand English, but to speak it, well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an interpreter or translator in your office able to interpret into English on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His or her name?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tanja Saric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at these documents. Save for one -- I think they've all got translations now, and I wanted you to have a look at them simply to confirm that this is the range of written communications that were being received and sent. Your Honours will find that they are page numbered in the bottom right-hand corner, so if the witness looks at page 2 and we look at page 1, this is September 1992, a report on enemy forces deployed in a particular area. We can see at the bottom that there's a handwritten remark that you should prepare a detailed report. That's the sort of tasking that you occasionally received, was it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I sent such reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pages 3 and 4, please. You look at page 4, Major. This is a handwritten document in your own hand, with instructions to people in Zepce and Kiseljak in November of 1992. So although you were then in Zenica, you were already requiring people as far away as Kiseljak; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From what I can see, this is one of the meetings that I mentioned yesterday about being held in the Operative Zone, Central Bosnia, and this is the invitation to those people in the intelligence service to report to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pages 5 and 6, instructions to Vitez, Novi Travnik, and Travnik, November 1992, to complete reports on the ground, signed by you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pages 7 and 8, this one is signed, and it says so in hand, dated the 1st of December, with a December reference number in the region of Serici. "No significant changes on behalf of the aggressor," and so on. A typical document you would have sent?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pages 9 and 10, the last document for 1992. You remember telling the Judges yesterday that documents were renumbered as from the beginning of December 1992. You'll notice that at the top of this one, as with the previous ones, there's a serial number for 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, could you tell the Chamber, what is the purpose of showing these documents to the witness, so we can follow you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. As I indicated, it's to show the range of documents that would exist, if we had access to all of them, and the range of responsibilities of this witness. And I'm doing it as a quickly as I possibly can. I also have to deal with, as you'll see from the last document, a rather important document, the date of which may have been uncertain yesterday but will be certain today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we see on the 24th of December, still with a 1992 serial number, commission of equipment for the reconnaissance squadron, of which you were, what, the commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, yesterday you reacted rather lovely to the mention of time, but I should nevertheless like to say that time is important in a case. And here we're not questioning the responsibility and functions of the witness; perhaps his credibility, but we already discussed it. So you should follow the Chamber when you're asked to put together your evidence in cross-examination and to try to cut it shorter, to make it more succinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am doing so, and it is succinct, I trust. I can't deal with documents much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we come to the next document, page 11 and 12, you can just confirm that that's another document directed to you. Page 13 is a translation of some significance of a document that recurs on several occasions. It's attached at the back of Your Honours' bundles, page 13. We've seen lots of these documents, and we had no translation of them yesterday. This is a document at your page 14, Major, which says there was no combat activity in the zone of responsibility of your brigade until a particular hour. If we look at pages 14, 15, and 16, we see three such documents for the same day. At page 17, we see a similar document for the 28th of February. Pages 18 and 19, we see another document simply signed by yourself, and I'm not going to take time on these. I just need them to be in evidence for later argument. At page 20, we see another document saying there was no activity. At 21 and 22, another document by yourself. And then at 23, a document as late as the 28th of March, saying that there was no activity in the area of the brigade. And then finally, and this is for completeness, pages 24 and 25, we see the document of which we had an inferior copy yesterday, which makes it quite clear that it was indeed on the 16th of April of 1993 that you were seeking data regarding the developments in Vitez. Now, that was the 16th of April. Is the position that you knew that things were developing in Vitez in accordance with a plan, Major?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should first like to answer the questions asked regarding the numbers of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Would you answer the question, please, rather than answering the questions which you'd like to answer. Would you repeat the question, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the position on the 16th of April that you knew things were developing in Vitez in accordance with a plan?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know what was going on, and that is why I sent this invitation. But you should know that it is very, very close, so that you can hear everything that goes on. And that was why I requested information, to really know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were subsequently to work for Blaskic. Were he to have described you as his eyes and ears, would that accord with your understanding of your position?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did, or had I been involved in those matters, I would have probably understood it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this war was over, on the 24th of December of 1996, you received a very high award, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Christmas Eve 1996.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't really know whether that was the date, but I was not awarded only one declaration; I was awarded several declarations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the declarations you were awarded was awarded by President Tudjman; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was the order of the Croatian trefoil, which is the eighth most senior of all military declarations awarded; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's conferred on Croatian and foreign citizens for exceptional contributions to the Republic of Croatia made in war, under an immediate threat of war, or in extraordinary peacetime circumstances. Can you explain, please, if you have the citation in mind, what it was that you had done to benefit Croatia in the time of war?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for that part, I suppose my role in liberation operations that were performed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, liberating the Croat territories and Muslim territories from the Serb aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your position that your role, described as a liaison officer, was still in fact an important intelligence role, Major, even when you were working for Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, when I worked for Colonel Blaskic, I was the liaison officer with international organisations. And afterwards, after that, I was again posted to another place. I was transferred to the post of the commander of the intelligence department, so that these two parts of my role in the war do not have much in common.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you been trained in intelligence before the war?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have any contact with military establishments, or was I involved in any military occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we distribute 1146.2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's being distributed, as to the Convoy of Joy, just to save time, do you agree with Mr. Whitworth's assessment that there was an element in the reaction of the Croats at the Convoy of Joy; there was an element of trying out the new British battalion to see how far they'd let you go?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as Whitworth is again concerned, and dealing with the killing of Dobrila, do you accept that although a paper was prepared at some stage about that killing, and he says waved in front of him, it was never actually presented to him, the report?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for that part, I've already said. The murder of Dobrila, we never managed to bring that investigation to a close, because we simply could not gain access to all the necessary evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croat side maintained that a Muslim had crossed the lines, gone to a Croat area to fire on the woman, and then returned, and that was a version that the British would never accept, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the investigating team was explaining, because I was a coordinator during the investigation of that murder, so that I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you're going to say you don't know, that's all I'm going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- finish my answer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- 6.2, a milinfosum for the 18th of July, in the middle of the page: "Darko Gelic, the Operational Zone Central Bosnia liaison officer, has confirmed that the HVO are attacking Stari Vitez and that the artillery barrage was the preliminary phase." Do you remember giving that information, and was it correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of information is all in all correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3, you also confirmed the helicopter flight into Vitez reported on the day before was bringing in some very -- some piece of very important equipment. Helicopter flights were used for ammunition as well as for personnel, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On a regular basis? On a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't on a regular basis. It depended on the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The killing of the UNHCR driver was said by Duncan to have been committed with a 12.7 millimetre rifle of a type seen in possession of the HVO from a position Whitworth was able to identify -- sorry, at a position Whitworth was able to identify and from a position that Duncan said was an HVO position. You don't challenge any of that, do you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, sir, in the British battalion, immediately after, that is, immediately after, two or three minutes later, after the murder of the driver, I was told that I had killed him. If you compare it with what you are saying now, then -- could somebody draw the conclusion after two or three minutes who was the murderer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. 1147.3. You see, you've presented a picture to the Judges that really all the attacks were by the BiH. You would accept, wouldn't you, as this document is now going to confirm, there was both the attacks, as we've seen, and also the threats of attacks, here on a document of the 26th of July: You, Darko Gelic, claim that if the BiH attack Vitez, the HVO will retaliate by shelling Zenica. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. All these documents you are showing to me, they are all interpretations of somebody's words. These are not my words. And it never occurred to me to use such words, simply because at that time we had neither ammunition, nor a possibility, nor an opportunity to do such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which case it may have been incorrect information but nevertheless given by you. Did you say anything to the officers at the time along the lines of "There would be the shelling of Zenica," please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We've heard from an officer called Verhoeven that you didn't cooperate in the movement of persons from Stari Vitez by the Red Cross and that you held it up for a time. True or false?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depended on the conditions and the circumstances we found ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that might be true?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't be true. I said it all depended on the possibilities and situation on the ground, because you must know that we had hundreds of wounded we had to transfer, and it depended on such moves. If we do not let one, they will not let others. So the Muslims were blackmailing us, whether they would allow our wounded to pass through, and that is what everything hanged on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we have Exhibit 1187.2, please. I'm sorry not to have given you earlier notice. Yes. Can you put it on the -- can you withdraw that and I'll come back to it in a minute. 1201.1, please. We can deal with these now quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 121.1, a milinfosum for the 14th of September, makes it quite clear, doesn't it, Major, that you are reported as saying that: "The HVO troops involved in the recent fighting to capture the Grbavica feature were from the 2nd Battalion of the Viteska Brigade," although you declined to say whether those troops came from Busovaca. So that would be Cerkez' troops; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You're recorded as saying that the troops involved in fighting to capture the Grbavica feature were from the 2nd Battalion of the Viteska Brigade. Cerkez' troops?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot remember this document. I cannot recall saying exactly that. I might have said something like that or what the document says here, but I can't really remember what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it true that Cerkez' troops were involved in the attack on the Grbavica feature; "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a part of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we come back to the other documents. Sorry, can that go back on the ELMO, please, on the second page? That's 1187.2. It's an earlier document, but not -- it's August. This is another summary, a daily summary prepared by a Mr. Watkins, and he makes the point on the second sheet, VI -- sorry, 6, that: "VI was refused permission to pass Kruscica, and when the HVO operational command was informed, the liaison officer stated that Colonel Blaskic had problems with the Viteska Brigade commander, Mario Cerkez, obeying orders. " Do you remember telling them that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, the question is whether Mr. Mario Cerkez put it that way. I don't believe it, because his brigade had its area of responsibility and had its commander there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you think of anything you may have said to this reporting officer that he may have misinterpreted to suggest that Blaskic had problems with Cerkez obeying orders?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that the Vitez Brigade had -- was posted to a particular place. It had its area of responsibility. Every battalion commander had his area of responsibility. When I went to individual areas to organise the passage for some international organisation, then each one of those commanders would logically try to deny such passage at first. But then either at my urging or Colonel Blaskic's insistence, they would permit that. But perhaps it may not have happened within the particular segment of time that they asked for it, and shall we say 1300 hours, but it did happen later the same day or perhaps the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go any further than to draw to your attention that this is a suggestion that he had "problems" with Mario Cerkez, not "a problem". That doesn't help you at all, does it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, because I'm telling you such things did not happen only in the area of responsibility of the commander of the Vitez Brigade; it happened all over the place. On repeated occasions, we had to travel with UNHCR trucks which transported not only food but also some other equipment, and our police could also establish that at some checkpoints. And that was why we simply did not -- we showed less trust at some checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept, Major Gelic, that you made it clear that the Vitezit factory would be blown up, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say something in that vein.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a comment here to an officer called Verhoeven; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was not a threat, sir. This was just a psychological influencing of someone. This is called psychological warfare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. There was, what, no serious intention to do this?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we done so, none of us would have survived it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you accept that this was a threat that you were making on behalf of Blaskic on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat again. This was not a threat, and it was not done on a regular basis. I said it once during certain Muslim offensives against the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You accept that you said it to Verhoeven?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The documents, Your Honour, are 1207.1. That is one document which is already in evidence. I shan't trouble with it. 1315.3, which deals with entries related to this witness on both the 8th and 9th of November, where the claim was he would blow up the Vitezit factory. Can we play a video now very shortly? It's 2238.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all. That's enough on that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a little earlier in October. That was a real threat, wasn't it, Major?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What had happened was a defensive position. That was to destroy one part of the hill in order to defend our forces. That is, the Muslim forces had taken about 100 metres of terrain there and in such a way that they had control over the town of Vitez. They could shoot at anything moving in the town, and this is why this operation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two other documents and then I'm done, 128 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other documents. 1286.1, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to explain a little more what he meant by "a defensive position". Is he saying that the words that he spoke which came across in the video explaining the attack were -- is he saying that this was by way of the Croats acting in defence? Would you explain that for me?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly correct, Your Honour. In that area, the Muslim forces had carried out an attack and taken a position which was slightly above the position which had been attacked. This was part of their overall effort to take the Vitezit factory. They broke through our lines. We had to withdraw to a lower position. But in order to gain some kind of a tactical advantage, we had to move our forces there, but we were unable to do so because there was open terrain there. So any soldier that would attempt any movement would be killed. So we had to destroy that area of the hill so that we would level the field, so to speak, so that we could continue with the defence of the terrain that we controlled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1286.1, the 5th of November, front page. Over half the way down, a report, Major, the beginning of November, that you told the ECMM monitors that the HVO did not fight for Vares because of the superior forces of 2 and 3 BiH Corps, and that according to you, the BSA did not interfere because of an agreement they had made with BiH about territory taken in the past. Then there was a problem about whether the BSA would let civilians or military pass. But it's true, isn't it, that there was an agreement, of which you were aware, between the BSA and the HVO that led to the failure to fight for Vares?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I had said before. Unfortunately, Your Honours, I find myself forced to repeat things. This is an interpretation of someone's words. I certainly did not put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then how should you have put it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perhaps have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might object, I think the question is misleading because the English actually says: "According to him, the BSA did not interfere because of an agreement they made with the BiH." Not "with the BSA", "with the BiH about territory taken by the BSA in the past." So I just object to the question on the grounds that it's misleading and it mischaracterises the contents of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second sentence reads like this, and I'll read it slowly: "According to him, the BSA did not interfere because of an agreement they had made with the BiH about territory taken by the BSA in the past. A problem that the HVO is facing in this area at this moment is the fact that BSA permits the passage of civilians out of Vares but does not allow all of the HVO forces to pass, so that some are still in the Vares pocket." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpretation was very fast, so I didn't quite catch all of it. Can I please have it read one more time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I wonder if we're going to be assisted much by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I put it in as part of the background, but it's there documented. The last document, 1296.2, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, you've heard me suggest that you had made references to this threat to blow up the Vitezit factory on several occasions, not just the once of which you speak. Here is a document dated the 10th of November, an ECMM document. On the second page, please, item 3: "BritBat was informed by Darko Gelic they would blow up the Vitez ammunition factory before the BiH were able to take it. HVO say they will give BritBat two hours' notice before doing so." And then there was a comment by the reporting officer. Did you tell BritBat that they had or they would be given two hours to evacuate?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look. Can you please just refer me to the date again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. This is a report dated the 10th of November, and whether it reports events that day or the previous day is perhaps not always entirely clear, but it certainly dates it as the 10th.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly right, Mr. Prosecutor, this could have been a day or two -- actually, two or three days earlier. Your Honours, this was the situation: As I said, these were not threats. This was part of psychological warfare which had to be conducted in that area, and this was uttered at the time when we were brought at such risk that we had no way out. And it was clear that Alija Izetbegovic had ordered that nobody was to be let -- leave the Lasva Valley alive if he was captured, that they all had to be killed or their throats cut. And again these were not threats, this was psychological activity. And we knew that the British were also visiting with the Muslim side and they would be able to convey this message. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... threat. What was it intended to be? What was the purpose of it, if it wasn't a threat?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was made as a psychological -- for psychological effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the psychological effect to be?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect was to stop the Muslim forces from advancing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: By means of a threat; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a threat. A message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, as his eyes and ears, aware of Blaskic having the detonators and so on at the factory filmed by independent television news; were you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, again I have to tell the Prosecutor I was not Mr. Blaskic's eyes and ears at the time. I was his liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were you aware that he was filmed showing how the thing was going to be blown up? Please, "yes" or "no". You seem to have dealt with a lot of the -- what is it -- messages, knowing of the messages.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of this particular message by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told Sir Martin Garrod, on about the 28th of December, as he thought, that Kordic had assumed a new function and that that function related to General Roso. Do you remember telling Sir Martin Garrod, one of the ECMM monitors, that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe Sir Martin Garrod interpreted it to himself, because Mr. Kordic never got such a function, never had one. And you said that this was on the 28th of January. I do not wish to comment on Sir Martin Garrod's state at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say he interpreted it because Mr. Kordic never got such a function. Never got what function, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't identified if yet. What do you understand me to be referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that he was appointed to something with Roso. That is, I believe, what you had said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't spell it out. Do you remember now what it was that he was apparently appointed to, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat again: Mr. Kordic was not appointed to any military function or duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you couldn't explain, I suppose, how you would have said -- or how you would have been understood by Sir Martin Garrod as saying that he, Kordic, was Assistant Chief of Staff to General Roso, thus making him number 3 in the military hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I do not want to comment on Sir Martin Garrod's state of mind, but whenever we would sit in the office -- I have to say this, unfortunately -- we consumed certain drinks and we held conversations while doing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't hold back. If you want to say that one of the witnesses who gives evidence is under the influence of drink, nobody's going to mind your saying it. Is that what you want this Tribunal to think, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do? You want to say that Sir Martin Garrod's perception was affected by drink?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness finally have, for completeness, what we've had before but now has the front page, 1147.6. It's in the English translation still only at the moment, but we will obtain the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you only speak limited English, Major, if you'd like to look at it, you'll see that, although only in translation, this deals with the various orders of declarations provided for members of the Croatian army, and we can see that number 2 was the order in respect of which Mr. Kordic was to be honoured, and you were number 8, conferred on Croatian and foreign citizens for exceptional contributions to the Republic of Croatia made in war, under an immediate threat of war, or extraordinary circumstances in peacetime. You knew that what you were doing for Herceg-Bosna, or for the HVO, was also doing something for Croatia, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that because you all understood, certainly at the beginning, that the aim was to unite this part of Central Bosnia with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not want to confirm such a statement. We were fighting to create an area where we -- the Bosnian Croats would have a decent and safe life, not to unite with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew, of course, that Croatia was providing troops and senior officers to this fight, such senior officers including people like Roso and Praljak; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, and Your Honours, Messrs. Praljak and Roso were the HVO officers. And not only did the Croatian troops not come, but I don't have any information that they ever did. They certainly did not come to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, let me just confirm, because various bits of the material you provided yesterday were entirely fresh to this Tribunal. It's not accepted that there was an attack on Zenica when you say there was. There was no reason for the Bosnian Muslims to attack Zenica, in which they held a majority. The only attack on Zenica, I'm going to suggest to you, was a limited one by the HVO initially.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was not so. First of all, they attacked the Croatian Defence Council in Zenica, and it is perfectly well-known when and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, just a few questions. You've been asked about a lot of materials which we didn't cover with you, but let me just ask you this. First of all, with respect to the matter of military declarations, were you aware that the order of the Croatian trefoil was also conferred upon President Izetbegovic, Prime Minister Haris Silajdzic, and Minister Ganic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this in connection with military activities that occurred in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was for the cooperation between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. I don't know exactly why they received them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you gave some testimony in connection with the death of the UNHCR driver, Boris, who we believe to be Boris Zevracic, but you couldn't identify his surname. You said that, and I'm paraphrasing what you said, "I was told that I had killed him." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the exact words Mr. de la Mota from UNHCR, in the presence of Mr. Duncan, two or three minutes after the killing, told me this. He said, "Sir, you killed him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean you personally or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was referring to me personally. He pointed a finger at me and he said, "Sir, you killed him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was just two or three minutes after the incident?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I can explain the reason why I was there with BritBat. I went there to seek assistance regarding the attack by the Muslim forces from the Zabilje area. I arrived in a vehicle in front and I drove to the camp and the Muslims there took it away from me. I was protected by my driver, and we almost forced our way in. The British soldiers did allow us in. And this is when the killing in Stari Vitez took place. De la Mota was on the way. And two or three minutes passed, and he pointed his finger at me and he said, "Sir, you killed him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he had come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made no further comment, and he said that he will have no further cooperation with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were interrupted in giving an answer related to the killing of Dobrila Kolaba. Could you just tell the Court what you had wanted to say when you were cut off, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation indeed tried to determine all the facts. When I arrived at the house where she had been killed, there was no body there. I talked to the British officers who were there. They said that they had removed a body, that they were very sorry that she was killed. I asked about what other houses were around and from which of the surrounding houses a shot could have been fired. Then they pointed approximately the direction from which the shot or the burst of fire had come. And according to them, she was shot by us, a single bullet, even though we saw several pock marks on the facade. And I told them, after they had shown me the direction that they thought that the shot had come from, I told them that our forces were not in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were asked some questions about various documents that you were shown, and I wonder if the registrar might put before you Exhibit Z672.2A. You were also asked some questions about the enumeration on these orders, and I wonder if I can ask the registrar to locate Exhibit D17/1.20 while you're looking at that document, Major. Now, Major, have you ever seen this document before? Can you confirm for the Court whether it is or it is not authentic, a real document. Can you help us out on that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, I can say that I sent a similar document to this one, or perhaps this one; however, there is no signature of mine there. But a document similar to this one I did send to the chief of counterintelligence. And if I may just add one more thing regarding the registration numbers. I did not use a single protocol book. The Prosecutor didn't allow me to elaborate. You see that the duty operations officer uses one code number, and I used one for reports, one for information, one for daily reports. So they are not from the same log book or protocol book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I wonder if the registrar could put on the ELMO the Croatian version, first page of the Croatian version, of an order signed by Commander Totic on the 5th of April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we can see on this document, sir, it's dated April 5th, 1993, but the number is 703/93. Can you throw any light on that for us, because that appears to be a number which is later, sequentially, than the number that appears on Exhibit Z672.2A, although that document is dated apparently 11 days later.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how that change in sequence or how that apparently illogical sequence came to be, the numerical sequence?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same as the clarification that I have just given. There were several books of protocol, or log books, and the brigade commander has his own log book. And if he personally produced a document, it would be entered there; and if it wasn't, then it would be logged in another one. However, there is also a joint log book. So there is not a single log book where the documents are entered, so the numbers do not necessarily reflect the sequence in which these documents were sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm through with that document. Just three other sets of questions, and I'll be done in just a minute or two. I wonder if you could be shown a copy of the photograph that was identified as Exhibit Z2546. I actually have a copy of it here. We can just put it on the ELMO, if I may. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person on the left of the picture, sir, who's that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was one of the British officers who was with us. I cannot recall exactly who. This was a long time ago, and thousands of faces have gone through my mind, but I think that this was one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person to the right, around whom you have your arm, I believe, is the British officer's interpreter, a Muslim lady; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My arm is actually on the side; and yes, it is an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just one question in connection with Exhibit Z812.1, which was an ECMM weekly summary for the week of April 17th to the 24th, 1993. Let me just read out to you, sir, a section on page 2, a very short section. I just invite your comments on this, if I may. "The regional centre in Zenica was requested by a so-called group of Mujahedins in order to mediate in the negotiations to exchange the Croat hostages for the Arabic prisoners. The Muslim extremist factions in Zenica were working in the town without any apparent control, people arrested, actions against CRO, or Croatian or Croat buildings, assault to CD radio." Were there any Muslim extremist factions actually arresting people and basically operating without any visible control in Zenica at the time that you say the attack was launched by the ABiH on that city, sir? Or to be more accurate, upon the HVO and Croat civilians in that city.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the prewar situation is concerned, that is, before the Muslims attacked Croats in Zenica, on a number of occasions they were killing our men, either in cafes or in front of coffee bars, in intersections. They threatened people, either that they would expel them, that they would kill them, or something like that, and especially after the attack of the ABiH forces, which together with the Mujahedin attacked Croats in Zenica. Not only did it result in Croats being arrested, but I can tell you about a case which happened before my brother was arrested. About 15 Mujahedin got out of a van in Mala Broda, near Cedomir Jonic's house. They fanned out in the area of three to four hundred meters, they searched houses, and there are women and children almost in every house. They made them leave their houses, they frightened them, they ransacked homes, and this was something that was happening day and night. The Muslims who lived in the surrounding houses would send messages out to the Mujahedin, and then the special police or some police would show up to allegedly protect people and calm things down. However, whenever the Mujahedin would show up, these police would just withdraw, so there was no protection whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one final set of questions relating to Exhibit Z881.1, about which you were asked, if I may. I actually have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, we can just put page 2 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 2, please. Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Major Gelic, I appreciate this is in English, so I'll read it slowly. And let's go over each one of these things here. It says: The Vitez LO, that's liaison officer, confirms the following details on the 4th Battalion HVO MP, meaning military police, aka, which means also known as, Jokeri, and in brackets appear the words "Black Knights." First, isn't it true that the Jokers were actually a subunit of a company known as the 4th Battalion of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, therefore, the comment that's made that the 4th Battalion of military police is also known as the Jokers. Is there any substance to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This whole excerpt is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the comment that the Jokers are also known as the Black Knights, or I believe it's in Croatian, Crni Vitezovi, that's not correct either, is it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Vitezovi were actually not even military police, were they, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the comment goes on to say that if this is the case, then certain conclusions could be drawn, after the observation that this unit apparently comes under the direct control of Dario Kordic and is under the local control of Tihomir Blaskic. Let me ask you, sir: Was Dario Kordic ever in a position of responsibility or authority with respect to either the 4th Battalion of military police, its subunit, the Jokers, or the Vitezovi, as far as you know, from all of your experience in the headquarters of the HVO for approximately nine months?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Kordic never had any authority, nor could he command any of these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Major, I'd like to ask you a question. If Mr. Kordic had given you an instruction to do something, what would be your reaction?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I would first have to report to my superior and seek his permission; that is, it would have to be my superior commander who would have to authorise me to comply with the orders of somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I put one unusual request, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Another question, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was just when this document was presented. Just one simple question. I may avoid a couple of witnesses. Just asking one simple question, the same which was asked based on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The question should be whether Mr. Cerkez was in any command position towards the mentioned units on those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow you to ask it, but you've heard the question, Major Gelic. Was Mr. Cerkez in any command position in relation to the Jokers or any of those other units which were mentioned in the document?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for coming. You are released, free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Colonel Zvonko Vukovic. However, while we're waiting for him to be brought in, I should like to say that when Colonel Vukovic agreed to testify here in The Hague, he also asked that he be placed under -- he asked for some protective measures, for reasons that were listed in the motion that was submitted. However, meanwhile, Colonel Vukovic has said that he gave it a second thought, changed his mind, and should like the hearing to be public, and therefore we should like to withdraw our motion for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While he's arriving, can I tell the Chamber this: First of all, Mr. Scott will be dealing with this witness, and unless the Chamber expresses disapproval, I shan't necessarily be in for all the evidence, because there are things to do. The second thing: We've received a summary this morning of the next witness the Defence intend to call. For some reason, a letter of which we've now been given a copy notifying us, I think, last Friday that they were going to call him this week as opposed to next week, it hasn't yet been traced in the building. It may be in the building or it may not yet have arrived, I don't yet know, a fax. But in any event, I will just alert the Chamber to the fact that we're in considerable difficulties, not being in any sense alerted to the fact that that witness was going to be called next. But I'll see what the position is when I've been able to attend to the papers that I have in relation to these witnesses. Mr. Scott is now here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, we sent a fax last Friday to the Prosecution, I believe, and it outlined the anticipated order of witnesses for the next two weeks. And that followed on an earlier communication that we had sent regarding the expected witnesses for the next three weeks. And this witness was identified, I think, in all of those faxes, and in our last Friday fax, as witness number 3 for this week. We've also provided the summary of this witness's evidence by fax to the Prosecution yesterday, and I believe we sent a copy to the Court as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate this witness will be, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, between half an hour and an hour. I don't think that the examination-in-chief will take more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, before we begin, I have already explained to Their Honours that you thought about it and decided to testify in public, so that we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zvonko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on the 26th of January, 1964, in the village of Potkraj?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, the Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are married and have three children?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before this war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you lived in your native village, in the village of Potkraj, which is about seven kilometres away from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, west of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, we are getting a request from the interpreters for a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been a long time since I conducted examination, and I slightly lost touch. I'm sorry. I shall do my best not to repeat that mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, will you please also wait a little bit after you've heard my question, until it is interpreted, and then answer it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I was about to ask you: You and your family and other Croat families were expelled from your native village by the army of Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your house was burnt down, and you lost all the property that you had been acquiring for years?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We lost everything, I and my family, we lost everything there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, with the help of the community at large, you are repairing now your house and are planning to go back to your native place?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I'm planning to bring all these works to an end and go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few words about your earlier military service. You served your regular military service with the JNA between February 1985 to March 1996?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1986, sorry. And then between June 1988 to September 1991, you worked in Travnik for the Yugoslav People's Army as a professional noncommissioned officer. You were under a contract with them, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I applied when they had the public competition, and during that period of time I worked for the Yugoslav People's Army. I had a technical job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in September 1991, when the war broke out in Croatia, you left the JNA, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were one of the first members of the -- first JNA members who left the barracks in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you left the JNA when the HVO began to take shape, you were one of the first members and organisers of the HVO in the area, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I left the former JNA, I immediately placed myself at the disposal of the lawful, legal authorities in the municipality of Travnik, and the authority was shared by Croats and Bosniaks. In the municipality of Travnik, I had no contact with the Serb side during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time, at the time when you joined in the organisation of the HVO in Central Bosnia, you were captured by the Bosnian Serb army when you went to participate in negotiations on the 26th of April, 1992. They were to take place on the Vlasic mountain?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 26th of April, 1992, being a member of the army which had then already got the name of the Croat Defence Council, and Mr. Boris Matisic, president of the executive board of the municipality of Travnik, we together went to Vlasic after a previous agreement to talk to representatives of the Bosnian Serb army about the turnover of the barracks in Travnik and the military depot in Slimena. However, rather than to do as agreed, they tricked us. They immediately bound us up and escorted us to the prison in Stari Gradiska. And while we were there, we were ill-treated and beaten. When I returned, I immediately went for treatment in the Travnik hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were being treated for a heavy beating and the effects of that heavy beating that you were exposed to during your captivity by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last thing, I'm now referring to paragraph 7, about your military service. Between the 8th of August, 1997, to the 6th of September, 1999, you were the head of the Department for Rules of Conduct and Development in the Ministry of Defence in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During that period of time, 1997, I left my duty in the command of the 3rd Corps in Vitez and went to the Ministry of Defence of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had the rank of Colonel in the Federation army, you still have it, and at present you're on sick leave, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we shall move on to the organisation and chain of command in the military police of Central Bosnia at the time when you served with it. A moment ago, you told us that you were treated in the Travnik hospital for injuries you suffered when you were beaten by Serbs during your captivity. However, towards the end of May 1992, you nevertheless joined the HVO again?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I recovered or even before I was fully recovered, I left the hospital and went home for house care, so that about a month after my release, I joined the HVO again and placed myself at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you then became deputy commander of the HVO military police, which was then about to be set up for the whole area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: True. After I reported to them, I made contact with Mr. Ivan Lalic, who had already been appointed the commander of the regional military police for Central Bosnia. However, during that period of time, there was no command, that is, that commanded the regional police. The only one I found there at the time was Ivan Lalic, who had been designated -- who had been appointed the commander and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it had not yet taken shape. There wasn't even the command, that was not in existence yet. However, Mr. Ivan Lalic was then transferred, and in October of that year, that is, on the 15th of October, 1992, you replaced Mr. Ivan Lalic and became the commander of the regional military police in Central Bosnia; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. When Mr. Ivan Lalic went to take a new duty in Mostar in early October 1992, I was appointed the commander of the regional military police. And at that same time, the new commander, that is, myself, was tasked with reorganising the regional military police into the 4th Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, it was only when you became the commander that the proper organisation of the military police began. And you were involved with this organisation until the end of 1992, and by that time you managed to form not only your command but also to bring together quite a number of the force, so that the 4th Battalion of the military police had some 550 to 600 members by the end of November?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. When I was appointed on the 15th of October, 1992, we first undertook the setting up of the command itself, and then trying to use the existing military police forces which existed in municipalities alongside municipal commands. So we reorganised that military police into the 4th Military Police Battalion, and it now had the command of the 4th Battalion of the military police and it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, it's time for the break. Would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, we may take up where we stopped. So you began to tell us about the establishment, the instatement, of the 4th Battalion of the military police, and in paragraph 10 of our summary you say that first five companies were set up, and you indicated which were their areas of responsibility and you were asked something about that. You can then answer his questions in detail, all right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you will agree with this approach?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this organisation, the organisation, was an ongoing process. When Jajce fell, one of the companies ceased to function, but others were set up. So this was a process that underwent many changes; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for these companies which were set up, very briefly, every company had its commander?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who do they account to, these commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The commanders, during that period of time, accounted, administratively and logistically speaking, to the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police, that is, myself, and in their daily work the company commanders, on the ground -- that is, commanders of platoons, commanders of squads -- accounted to commanders of companies, or rather at that period of time brigades began to grow at the municipal level; that is, municipal brigades began to be formed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, it means that in places there were companies formed, and in some places, where there would be several platoons from different areas, they would all make one company; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is, companies and platoons were formed on the territorial principle, like before; that is, municipal headquarters, subsequently brigades. That is, say, depending on the area of the municipality and the size of the population which lived in the territory at the time. So depending on that, we tried to assess the necessary strength of the military police unit in those areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move on to the next item, paragraph 12. You commanded the 4th Battalion of the military police between the 15th of October 1992 and until the 18th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is, I was the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police during that period of time. And on the 17th I was issued a decree from the head of the administration of the military police from Mostar that I would not be a commander any longer, that my successor would be Pasko Ljubicic, and that I should turn over the duty immediately, which I did, and that I showed that report in agreement -- pursuant to the previous agreement. That is, I knew one month in advance that this would happen, that I shall report it to the administration of the military police for further posting. And the head of this administration intended to appoint me to one of the offices in the administration of the military police, and I had agreed to that almost a month before it actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, on the last day that you still had the post of the commander before Pasko Ljubicic took it over, an unfortunate incident happened, and a person, an individual who was working in close cooperation with you, was killed. That is your driver, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th of January, 1993, Beber was killed. He was the driver of the 4th Battalion of the military police, who served as my personal driver. And that same evening, the criminal investigation department of the service of the 4th Battalion, together with the MUP of the municipality of Travnik and the military police of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time conducted the investigation, but it never came to a court hearing. According to some information that I received later, I believe that I was to be assassinated that same day when he was killed. It happened on January 18th, in Travnik. At that time the BH army already was fully controlling those parts, that is, that part of the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, so although you were to go to a new duty in Mostar, you did not take up that office, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not take up that office, because when I received the decision that I was to hand over my previous duty, I was to report, and I was to report within a reasonable period of time, that is, of some 15 or 20 days, to my new duty. But in late January, after I turned over my previous duty, a conflict, fighting, broke out between the BH army and the Croat Defence Council in Kacuni, that is, in the municipality of Busovaca. And it took some time, so that I could not report then, because all the roads had been blocked by that time and one could not safely go through to Mostar. And I therefore reported about that to the administration where I was to go, where I was to report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last questions are about this in chapter E, which says subsequent assignments, paragraph 14. So you could not leave to take up your new duty and Colonel Blaskic, as the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, he appointed you to a different duty, didn't he? What was that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th of January, 1993, when the fighting had ended, the fighting that began in the end of January, in late January 1993, in Busovaca, at that time General Blaskic was in Kiseljak, and that day he was not in Vitez, at the headquarters in Vitez. And I was then appointed by Colonel Blaskic at the time to become the assistant commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia for Home Guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a new office. It did not exist before that, did it? So you were tasked with forming a service which had not been in existence before that; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I also had said that I would rather stay there and not change the decision and go to Mostar, so that I was at the free disposal. And this newly-established office, I think it was the commander of the Main Staff about to be formed on the basis of the organisation which was being developed at that time by the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to organise the Home Guards force in the Operative Zone, Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Home Guards force, as it was conceived and as it was supposed to be organised, that was never brought to an end. This process was only begun. On the 18th of February, when I was ordered to do that, we first, as instructed, undertook to set up Home Guard formations. We held several meetings with officers who were to command those units and defence officers which were to mobilise men for these units. Meanwhile -- and that was the period of time -- that was about a month, month and a half. What we know already happened, that is, that fighting broke out in Vitez on the 16th of April, so this process came to a halt and there was no way -- there was no possibility to proceed with this organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the beginning of the fighting in Travnik in 1993 put an end to what you had begun to do, organising the Home Guard units?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Chamber has already heard a great deal about the joint command which was set up towards the end of April 1993 after a ceasefire agreement had been reached. That is paragraph 15 in our summary. However, after this joint command of the forces of the HVO and the army of BH was set up at the level of the Operative Zone of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you became one of its members, didn't you, of that command?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in the beginning, I referred to the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia set up a commission, and it included, at the outset, Mr. Zoran Pilicic and Mr. Marko Prskalo, who later on, after returning from one of those meetings, were both wounded. After that, that team -- or, rather, later on an understanding was reached between the 3rd Corps and the headquarters of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia to appoint me to the joint command, and its seat was in the municipality of Travnik or, to be more -- and Mr. Franjo Nakic was appointed to the same commission, Mr. Vlado Juric, and my humble self was also appointed to it. And Mr. Vlado Juric worked together in this joint command. We were operations officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the head of the command of this joint command were Franjo Nakic, on one side as the HVO representative, and Dzemal Merdan as an officer of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it, and there were several of his officers too?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So Mr. Franjo Nakic and Mr. Dzemal Merdan headed it. And in addition to Dzemal Merdan, there were two more operations officers in the 3rd Corps and one liaison officer from each side who were responsible only for establishing communication. That is, there was one liaison officer on the BH army side and one on the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the developments on the ground in spite of the ceasefire agreement, eventually resulting in the fact that the joint command could not obtain any good results because you had to deal with a number of minor incidents, and so that the whole idea about setting up the joint command was somehow diverted to a different course?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we formed this joint command representing the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone, the commanders of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia and the commander of the 3rd Corps had signed an order, and that order said that the aim was to plan military operations in relation to the army of Republika Srpska. And in that -- we began, therefore, to draw up a plan for a joint operation which was to be carried out in [indiscernible]. It, however, never took place because daily at that time, and that was already May 1993, from one day to the other incidents began to occur, all sorts of problems arose, so that some problems jointly and with the [indiscernible] of the International Community, that is, ECMM and UNPROFOR, we had to go out into the field every day. And Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan would always go out together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to the next topic, that is, persecution. In this case, Colonel Vukovic, we've heard a great deal about persecutions. At the beginning, when you gave us your particulars, you mentioned your example and told us how you had been expelled from your home. Tell us, please, throughout the period of time when you held different military offices and while you commanded the 4th Battalion of the military police, did you receive any order at all that the HVO should persecute either Muslims or members of some other ethnic groups or peoples?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can claim, under full responsibility as an officer, that at that time the command of the Operative Zone, Central Bosnia, never. And not from anyone, not from my military superior or from a civilian politician, did I get any order in writing or oral which would show the desire to expel or duty to expel Muslims from the areas in which we lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, have you ever heard that anyone publicly or privately advocated or promoted inadvertent comments on this specific policy?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can repeat it only that nobody ever asked me to do that or ordered me to do that, nor did I order or instruct my subordinates while I was with the 4th Battalion military police, nor after I turned over that duty. So I never heard any such thing, never told me any such thing, nobody ever requested any such thing from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've mentioned military and political factors, and this brings us to paragraph 18. Tell us, please, while you commanded the 4th Military Police Battalion, who issued orders to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, in the beginning I told you how companies and platoons were organised, the operative daily orders, who issued operative daily orders, and what were my powers in terms of the organisation of the military police, the 4th Battalion, and then its organisation and companies. So in my daily work, I accounted to the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, but all the tasks, all the orders that were issued, were issued through the commanders of platoons, that is, squads on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, I would like to ask the following question of the witness: Considering his rank within the military hierarchy -- he was a colonel -- does he seriously think that the military live -- cut off from the rest of the world amongst themselves without any relations with politicians, with political structure, political objectives that are set out by the political structure, and that's the case in all countries in the world? Colonel Vukovic, you knew what were the objectives you were fighting for, and you knew who was setting these objectives? You were not just fighting for the sake of fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Your Honours, at that time I was not such a high-ranking officer to have any contact with the political life. As an officer, as a commander, at that time I was nowhere near them, nor was I under their orders. That is what I wanted to say. That is one thing. Secondly, I was not a colonel at the time in 1991. I was an NCO, a noncommissioned officer in the former army, and it was gradually -- in the course of this war, which was not to our liking, I gradually was promoted, I moved up, and this is what I am today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were a part of the military hierarchy. You were a commander, you were receiving orders from your superiors. So my question is the following: The people that were above you at any level in the army you belonged to, did these people, these superiors, did they have contact with politicians? Were you aware that they had contact with politicians and there was, indeed, a political objective that was being pursued in what we have to call a war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As regards political objectives, I did not have an opportunity to listen to them. What we had were our daily tasks and problems we solved, and my goal or my primary goal was to first join those units. And when the HVO was formed, then my prime goal was the defence against the Serb aggressor, because I lived in an area which was completely surrounded, that is, the Serb enemies surrounded them from three sides. And on Mount Vlasic, Mount Vlasic, the Serb aggressor, the former Yugoslav People's Army, their reservists had already taken possession of that mountain in February 1993, so that our movement in the area where I lived was restricted not due to the beginning of the war in April or May -- it depends -- but in early February 1992. As of early February 1992, I had to use completely new paths to get to my home, so as of the latter half of February. Now I'm trying to explain with regard to our points of contact with the Serb army, and that was the hostile army, my family, my wife, my parents, we were all there, and what I was concerned with was only to resist the Serb aggressor at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The territory you were defending, how did you define that territory?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the early days of the war, the front against the enemy army, the army of Bosnian Serbs, we took up those front lines. We did not have to go eight or ten or twelve kilometres from home. We took our positions immediately above our homes, when we tried to set up guards and to form the front line. At that time, we dug a trench here and there. We introduced duty. We tried to chose some commanders, to post commanders, and it was that we spent most time and effort doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, let us go back to where we were and to add to what His Honour has just asked you.
