utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you shed any light on why someone you describe as a political figure would become involved with the military police in arranging the return of a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it is misrepresented. I do see that Mr. Dario Kordic is mentioned here, but I really cannot comment on this document because I would have to read it. But perhaps he intervened through somebody else. I did not have the information that he interceded, intervened, directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just below that, sir, before we leave the document, it says: "On the 17th of November, 1992, the military police were in charge of the security of the staff, the Presidency, and logistics." I take it, sir, that at this time the Presidency included Mr. Kordic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This is related to the report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's right under the earlier reference -- immediately following the earlier reference to Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that. I see that this document is military police from -- it was sent by the military police in Kakanj to the military police in Kiseljak, and the Kiseljak military police, the commander of the military police company. And in Kakanj, there was only one platoon of the military police, so they report to the commander of the company, and I think --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to cut you off at this time. I think we're going to have to move forward. If Mr. Kordic's counsel thinks something needs to be clarified, they'll have a further chance to do that. I think we have to move on. If we could go down to Exhibit 356, Z356. Colonel, this appears to be again an order by you, dated the 11th of January, 1993, apparently only a few days before you were succeeded in this position by Pasko Ljubicic. You referred to each of the listed municipalities naming five members to special-purpose units of the military police. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may, I should really like to read it, not just scan it. But if you want me to comment on it, I should really read it carefully. May I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to cut you off, sir, but if I could direct your attention to the first paragraph. The rest of it, I can assure you, I will not ask you about the lower part of it. I want to be fair to you, but we also have to move along, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recall this document. This was a proposal to form an active-duty battalion of military police. We wanted to have some men and were planning to train them, and we thought that eventually we would have fully-trained military police -- well, checked that it's military police, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, sir, the authority of the command of the 4th Battalion of the military police extended throughout Central Bosnia to each of the municipalities listed at the top of this order; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the original -- Your Honour, I haven't -- as you know, I haven't been in the courtroom for all the testimony. I don't know if another witness has explained this or not, but the Court can tell me if they have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the bottom of the original, sir, is that information that was put on a document that shows that it was sent by something called packet communications?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, that was a system that was essentially like a combination of radio and fax machine?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the command of the 4th Battalion of the military police, I did not have the packet link. But when the need arose, I used the facility in Vitez, because they had it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was on Colonel Blaskic's headquarters when you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, when you use these documents and when you refer us to these documents, could you please specify the relevance of your questions to the witness in relation to the direct examination? Thus we could establish the link between cross-examination and direct examination, because here you're asking the witness to confirm a document. You ask specific questions, but we don't really see the relevance. So it would be a good idea if you could introduce the document in advance and tell us the relevance. Therefore, we could proceed more rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. In part, Your Honour, this document goes to -- there has been disputes throughout the case, as I understand it, as to the exact organisation of the military police and to the command of the various command groups in Central Bosnia, to such areas as Vares and Zepce and other places. That is one way in which this particular document is relevant. It's also relevant in that, Your Honour, I think other evidence in the case may tie up the involvement of some of these military police units and another of the incidents that the Court has heard about. I can't necessarily get all of that from this witness. In fact, given the nature of the long answers and the time, I can only tell the Court that some points on these documents are not being developed. But I will try to move -- I'm trying to move as quickly as possible. With that in mind, Your Honour, I think I can skip over, if you'll give me a moment, please, the next several exhibits, or at least the next exhibit which would be offered, Your Honours, largely again to show the inner relationship between the various military police units and the fact that authority did reach out to such places as Vares, referring now -- I suppose I might as well say it for the record -- to Exhibit Z362, to have certain Serb prisoners brought to Vitez for purposes of questioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move on, sir, to something called the Security Service or SIS. Now, that was part of the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the SIS?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies. I would not like to interrupt you at the time, but I never mentioned SIS in my examination-in-chief, and I fully support what Judge Bennouna said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll apply the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, when you left the command of the 4th Battalion military police in January of 1993, who selected Pasko Ljubicic to replace you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was a previous nomination, but on the 18th of November, the appointment came from Mr. Valentin Coric, head of the military police in Mostar, that he was appointed a new commander and that I should report to a new duty in the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what your new duties in the military police administration in Mostar were going to be?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I was supposed to be one of the officers in the general services of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Ljubicic became the commander, his deputy became -- well, did his deputy become a man named Marijan Nukic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but when I turned over the command of the 4th Military Police Battalion, I was the commander, and the second man was the assistant for the traffic police, and he was also my deputy. That was Dobrica Jonjic, and I did not follow his subsequent career development.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. When Mr. Ljubicic moved up from the 1st Active Company military police, was he replaced by Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Forgive me, Your Honour. In light of the time and the Court's ruling, I'm eliminating, just going through my outline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, have the time you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'll simply explain to the Court that in light of this person's senior position on Colonel Blaskic's Central Bosnia staff, there are certain matters of general relevance to the case which may fall, strictly speaking, outside of the scope that the Defence chose to include in their direct, that I would ask this witness, because I think he's in a knowledgeable position. But as I go through my outline, I'm now essentially eliminating much of that information -- or questions, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to, sir, if we can -- can you tell me where you were in mid-April 1993? By this time you were on Colonel Blaskic's immediate staff. You were based in Vitez, I take it, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me direct your attention starting about the 14th or 15th of April, 1993. Where were you at that time? What were your duties on Colonel Blaskic's staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, on Colonel Blaskic's staff, I had an office where I worked on the establishment of Home Guard units and establishing books on it. And I had my office hours, and after the office hours I would go back home, unless I was on duty, in which case I would stay at the headquarters for 24 hours at a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you, sir, on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993, as an assistant commander in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th I was in an apartment where I temporarily lived in Vitez. That was on the 16th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go into headquarters in Vitez that day?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: A little bit in the afternoon and a little bit in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time after the 16th of April, 1993, did Colonel Blaskic ever talk to you about the events at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I did not speak to Colonel Blaskic about Ahmici at all, because immediately after that, on the 23rd or the 24th, I joined that commission, which after the agreement was established, that was the joint command, and this is where I went on a regular basis. And I joined this commission after Mario Prskalo and Zoran Pilicic were wounded after they were coming back from the negotiations, and there were two members of this commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is this: You remained -- whatever your day-to-day duties on the joint command, you remained a member of Colonel Blaskic's senior staff. At any time after the events at Ahmici, did he ever talk to you about what had happened at Ahmici; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any reports or investigations of what had happened at Ahmici, in your role as a member of the senior staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I remained a member of the staff. I was not at the headquarters. I did not receive any information. I did not take part in an investigation of what happened in Ahmici. And our duties were such that every morning, from 8.00 on, we were in our offices in Travnik, and we would come back after 5.00, or sometimes even later. So I have very little information regarding events of that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear anyone in the Operative Zone's command staff voice the opinion, or the conclusion, or make the statement, that Pasko Ljubicic was involved in the crimes committed at Ahmici on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All I heard about Ahmici -- and I mostly heard about it from the joint commission, that is, from the joint command, where we would meet with the colleagues from the 3rd Corps, and I cannot say who participated and who did not, but the people with whom I talked were appalled by what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question remains, sir: During that time did you hear the opinion stated in the Vitez headquarters, in or about the Vitez HVO headquarters, that Pasko Ljubicic was one of the military leaders involved in the atrocities at Ahmici, as a member of the senior staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear this, that he was directly pointed out in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he directly pointed out?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody did directly, but as I said, when we talked to the people who were there in that joint command, they all would always say something. But there were no arguments offered, so I was not able to really enter into discussions with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you similar questions, but I think they can be "yes" or "no" answers, if possible, about two more individuals, or several. Did you hear that Mr. Anto Sliskovic was involved in the incident at Ahmici? Was that a subject of conversation in the Vitez headquarters, or among Blaskic's staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Vlado Cosic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Cosic. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, how about this Marijan Nukic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me put it to you that I think there's no question at this point that the events at Ahmici received worldwide attention; it was a tremendous atrocity by whoever committed it. All sorts of people -- the UNPROFOR, the ECMM, the European community -- were interested in knowing what had happened. There were communications with the Croatian government to know what had happened. You want this Court to believe that at no time after the events at Ahmici on the 16th of April, no one among Colonel Blaskic's senior staff talked about what happened at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer you this question, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I'd like to ask the witness how he came to know about the events in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You heard the Judge's question, sir? Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you hear about the atrocities in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: For the crimes in Ahmici, and the scope of it, but not specifically, I mostly heard from the colleagues from the 3rd Corps, with whom we were later on in the commission. And that was later on, on the 24th, 25th. I'm not exactly sure when, when it started. So most information I received from the colleagues from the 3rd Corps. They said that over 100 civilians, women and children, were killed there. But I wasn't there. I didn't hear about it from anyone. Perhaps there were some stories, until we saw the pictures and were able to verify it, because it was not -- at that time you couldn't believe everything, because there were -- people were telling all kinds of things then. We went to the church to see whether there were some prisoners of war. They were saying there were some prisoners of war kept in the church, but we saw that there were none there. But most information -- I got most of the information from the press and some from television, because that was a topic that was at that time present, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you if you had seen any reports or investigations about Ahmici. There was a particular report to Colonel Blaskic, allegedly, about the latter part of May 1993, from the SIS, and I believe the record would show presented to him by Ante Sliskovic. Is it your testimony, sir, that you never saw that report?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I state that I never saw any report from Ahmici, about Ahmici, compiled by anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to work with Darko Kraljevic while you were on the senior staff in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him. We would rarely meet, and we never did anything together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider him to be a -- what some of your colleagues might consider among the criminal element of the HVO in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I could say that some of his personnel could have been -- I don't know what they were all involved in, but I don't know exactly what I could tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the unit that Darko Kraljevic commanded?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were called Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could show you what's been marked as Exhibit Z1075.1. And for purposes of the stack or bundle, Mr. President, we've now jumped down several documents, I believe, but they should nonetheless be in order. If you go down till you hit 1075.1, please. I'm told the registrar has that, Your Honour. I'm sorry. If that could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, without wanting to interrupt, I think it's another SIS-related document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, it is. I'll say it, Your Honour; it is. It relates also specifically to Mr. Kraljevic, a man that this Court has heard extensive evidence about, I believe, among others. And I think if there's a relevant question that someone in the role of Mr. Vukovic -- or, excuse me, Colonel, should -- he may not be able to, but I can't know that -- shed some light on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you will look at Exhibit 1075.1. This appears to be a promotion of Mr. Kraljevic dated -- the document is dated the 18th of June, 1993, in which Mr. Kraljevic is being appointed as deputy chief for the Central Bosnia SIS centre. Do you have any information, sir, about why this Mr. Kraljevic would be promoted to the deputy chief of the Security Service in June 1993? Can you help us with that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I cannot comment on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at that time of any relationship between Mr. Kraljevic and Mr. Anto Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the relations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'll move on. Your Honour, I'd advise the Court that it probably hasn't been very pretty, but with a lot of on-my-feet editing, I think we have a chance of finishing the cross by 4.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back to the mention of Slobodan Praljak, who you indicated that you knew at one point had come from Croatia. Did you know, sir, that on the same time that you were on Colonel Blaskic's staff, that there were other -- at least one representative of the HV, the Croatian army, in Colonel Blaskic's headquarters? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I can state with full responsibility that during my time in the headquarters, that no officer from Croatia was in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Miro Andric? Isn't it true, sir, that he was an HV officer?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was. I don't have information about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know Mr. Andric at all? You didn't have any interactions with him in the Hotel Vitez headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have, but if we're referring to the same Andric, I know an Andric who was a Deputy Chief of Staff to Mr. [Realtime transcript omitted name Perkovic]. I cannot recall his first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, to who? To -- I'm sorry. I don't want to suggest a name to you if it wasn't correct, but who did you -- on whose staff?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll look over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you thought that he perhaps was a Deputy Chief of Staff to Mr. -- and even the transcript is blank. What did you say, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: If we're referring to the same person, I think his first name was Mario Andric. I don't know what his rank was. He was in the HVO Main Staff headquarters in Mostar. And at one point he stayed briefly in Central Bosnia. I only know that he was captured in Ravno Rostovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he doing in Central Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He didn't talk to me and he never interacted with me or with my job. That may have been around January 1993, or even December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to the time we talked about earlier this afternoon, when you were involved with Mr. Kordic and in the Central Bosnia command, was there someone named -- was there an officer named Zarko Tole -- I may be pronouncing the last name wrong. Forgive me -- that was the, if you will, the commander, the military commander, for what was being referred to as Central Bosnia, that preceded Colonel Blaskic? Do you remember that name, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I only remember that Zarko Tole was appointed. This is information that I received. I never saw him. And I know that very shortly, he was captured by the Serb forces in Bugojno municipality. So he was there briefly. I never had an opportunity to meet him or to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you to look to Exhibit 2360.18, and I don't know if it's in the bundle or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. In the interests of time, I'll simply put the photocopy on the ELMO, and if the witness could be provided the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that when Brigadier Tole was put in this position of the command of the Central -- what was then being called Central Bosnia, that that was on the order of General Bobetko of the army of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that, but I know that he was appointed. But I see for the first time now who it was that appointed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander of the southern front, General Janko Bobetko, the Croatian army command; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot comment at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition to appointing the brigadier, it also established an IZM Central Bosnia in Gornji Vakuf; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I see that in paragraph 1, and I know that in Gornji Vakuf there was some command post, but I never knew how and under whose orders this was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can help the Court in terms of just IZM. Do you know what, in Croatian military parlance, what is an IZM?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That would be a command post, a forward command post that was detached for specific tasks on a temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at the attached chart, sir -- we'll close with this -- this indicates a command post for Central Bosnia and the number of municipalities, including such places as Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik, et cetera. My question to you, sir: Isn't this, in fact, the Central Bosnia command that we've talked about today and what continued to be -- throughout these events, what really became then the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, originally established by Croatian General Bobetko? Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say whether this is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe this document is not true, the document that's marked before you? Do you have any reason to think this is not a true and authentic order by Janko Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a technical objection. This document has been tendered under a different number, without this chart. Now, shall we treat this as a new document? This is 2306.18. We have it in our files but without the attachment, so to me this attachment would seem to be a new document; at least we see it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, that the attachment is with, I hope -- if Ms. Verhaag is correct -- with the registrar's copy. It would have been tendered some time ago. I'm in the Court's hands. If it was not tendered then -- this is the form which I was using the document -- have been using the exhibit. If it hasn't been tendered, I would tender it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registrar says it's in the international armed conflict bundle, as it is here. It may be that the Defence haven't got it for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may presume, Mr. President, I think the point that Mr. Naumovski was making, that the exhibit that we have, Exhibit 2360.18, does not have any chart attached to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the original does, so your copy, it was omitted for some reason. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that, I conclude. That's my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. Mr. Naumovski, time is short because one of our number has to attend a meeting. Do you want to be very long with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honours. I am in a somewhat embarrassing position. There are quite a lot of documents here and some of them are quite new, but I shall try to be as brief as possible. Re-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, only a couple of questions more. You were asked a number of times, quite unnecessarily, I think, where did we have the interview in Split. It was in my room, in my suite, at Marjan Hotel?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said it was at a hotel, but I couldn't remember --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, quite fine. But we have to remember the interpreters. So these were the beginnings of an organised resistance across the Serb aggression; that was the time frame. And you spoke about the headquarters, about the Crisis Staff, and so on and so forth. So this is the spring of 1992, April, May, June; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree, then, that in May, for instance, the only lawful army in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in May, the JNA still kept the barracks at Travnik, at Kiseljak, Slimena, Kaonik, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was mentioned today, but that was a political body, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Political body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Matisic, who was a politician, a highly-appreciated politician in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he attended with you some meetings where efforts were made to organise men, materiel, raise funds, and so on and so forth, because you had begun the organisation from scratch, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the period of time when people like you volunteered to help with the organisation, because you knew that unfortunately war would break out in your areas, and you pooled your knowledge, some military, some logistical, some some other, in order to try to lay the foundations for what later came to be called the Croat Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly about these documents, you were shown one document, Z61. You looked at the signatures. You seem never to have seen it before, but it doesn't really matter. But you yourself mentioned that it transpired from this document that that meeting was of the basic organisations of the Croat Democratic Community in Zenica, Busovaca, Vitez, and Travnik and that it took place on the 17th of March, 1992. And among the signatures, we see featuring the signature of Mr. Dario Kordic and others and representatives of the municipal HDZ organisations or from relevant municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another document is Z62, where you agreed at a meeting that you should go and talk to Minister of Defence Susak in Croatia, and this is the period of time we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The 21st of March, yes. March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the beginning of what you were about to do in Central Bosnia, but when it is still at its embryonic stage, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, you were making preparations because you realised that there would be an aggression by whom?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: By the Serb or Chetnik army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the JNA, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the JNA too, which still existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that meeting, to your knowledge, did not take place?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it never took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There was also mention of another document, Z289, and the Prosecutor read out to you a part of it. You couldn't find your way around it, but it says something to the effect that Mr. Kordic is requesting that a car be returned to the command of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at a locality called Zivinice, and that document was signed by the commander of the military police, Zeljko Karic. I think I'm reading it correctly. Yes, Karic from Kakanj, isn't it? That is in Kakanj, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there, as it says in it, you said you had no knowledge of it, but this is something that is written by this gentleman from Kakanj, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to say something. I think I -- this document became clear to me. This is a platoon of the military police in Kakanj, and that platoon was a part of the 4th Company from Kiseljak, and it was the platoon commander who was reporting to the company commander. He reported to him daily on the activities of the platoon, and then it was the company commander who reported to me. So I really can say that I never laid my eyes on this document before. Perhaps I saw another document of a similar content, but I wouldn't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I won't ask you any questions about this document. But the Prosecutor read it, wanting to show that it was Mr. Kordic's office. That's why it was said. But it said here that the military police were in charge of the security of the staff and so on and so forth, and it is a man in Kakanj who writes that. So these are somebody's in Kakanj, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they must be in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, excuse me, just one more question. The recovery of this car that had been seized from the Muslims, that was no military operation; it was simply kind of a gesture? It wasn't a military operation, could I call it, even if it was so as this man says it is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it had happened, there would have been an order to return it to its owner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but I didn't really understand why did the Prosecutor show you this document, Z365. But some training in Capljine is mentioned, and Capljine is a town in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I may have omitted something, Your Honours, but I think that the witness must be already tired, and I would conclude therefore with this. Thank you, Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Vukovic. Thank you for coming. That concludes your evidence, and you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until half past 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.12 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of May, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
